Microstate thermodynamics overcomes the challenge of changing phase space volumes, enabling the calculation of precise time-dependent values for relevant variables. These variables include the number of particles, energy, pressure, and entropy, all expressed in terms of the initial and final states of the system. Furthermore, we've developed an innovative method for determining the phase space trajectory of a Hamiltonian system given initial and final conditions, with direct application to the free expansion process. We've verified our approach against established macrostate thermodynamics and simulation results for pressure-isothermal plots, as well as the bending universe model, which serves as a pedagogical tool to illustrate key concepts of thermodynamic development.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from connections and curvatures within a symplectic manifold framework, specifically focusing on globalization. We'll demonstrate how curvature graph weights can be explicitly defined through a hypergeometric function and an even simpler expression that combines it with a formula for the underlying connection graph weights. Notably, we examine a cotangent bundle case, leading to a substantial simplification of the curvature expression.

We explore solitary waves known as "nanoptera," characterized by exponentially small oscillations, in two precompressed systems based on the Hertzian model, particularly woodpile chains and diatomic chains with alternating masses. These solitary waves emerge from the Stokes phenomenon as special curves in the complex plane are intersected, producing exponential asymptotics approximations. Our analysis reveals that solitary waves in precompressed woodpile chains feature a single Stokes curve, accompanied by oscillations, whereas a diatomic chain exhibits two oscillatory contributions, cancelling out under certain mass ratios to produce localized waves, thereby confirming prior numerical and experimental observations on the phenomenon in non-precompressed diatomic chains. Nonetheless, an approach grounded in exponential asymptotics fails to accurately predict solitary wave formation for various mass ratios in precompressed diatomic chains.

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis explores the mechanics of a cosmic collider through two cases. Firstly, we consider a primordial feature that results in a quantum fluctuation generating a heavy field degree of freedom, yielding an observable signal for an extremely light dark matter field. Secondly, we examine a case of resonant inflation causing a broad feature in the primordial spectrum, producing an abundance of heavy states, such that their density exceeds the CMB scale even when the mass of these states exceeds the Hubble scale during inflation.

Consider a graph of even order G and its square extended graph G^2. Research indicates that if G is bipartite but not a perfect matching graph, then G^2 possesses a perfect matching. However, a distinct graph class exists where this rule holds true regardless of its properties. Specifically, investigating a unique graph class known as accordion graphs, it is proven that each accordion graph of order N possesses a perfect Hamiltonian cycle, along with a distinct quartic circulant lattice as its square. Moreover, it is demonstrated that if an accordion graph is chosen at random among those of order N and hamiltonian cycles, it will almost certainly not be isomorphic to its square. Finally, the computational complexity of verifying whether a given graph is an accordion graph or not is explored, leading to the conjecture that this task may be NP-complete.

We explore the open three-state quantum walk model within unstructured disorder and find that survival probabilities follow a distinct scaling law compared to earlier reported studies. Contrary to existing outcomes, our research reveals that the probability distribution of first return times can be broken down into two distinct parts, one that diminishes exponentially and another that decreases asymptotically at a rate proportional to $t^{-5/2}$. Furthermore, we observe that the late-time decay of the survival probability distribution exhibits a $t^{-2}$ rate that does not depend on the initial state, occurring universally across all three-state quantum walks regardless of their initial conditions. Additionally, we confirm that the scaling function governing this behavior remains independent of any specific model and that it is likely an intrinsic characteristic of discrete time quantum walks adapting to a particular type of continuous time random walk in the non-unitary regime.

This paper explores the benefits that self-supervised learning confers on Vision Transformer (ViT), distinguishing it from convolutional networks (convnets). Our findings show that self-supervised ViT features uniquely capture the semantic structure of an image, in contrast to supervised ViT features, which instead reflect the resolved input data. Additionally, our research reveals that self-supervised ViT features show diminished changes in response to minor alterations in data. Moreover, the vector space formed by these features exhibits distinct clusterable patterns and exhibits increased efficiency in representing image categories. To support these conclusions, our experiments were performed using a large-scale real-world dataset (ImageNet) and modest self-supervised training process (self-distillation with ResNet).

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and general. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we calculate the cosmological parameters including the equation of state parameter, ratio of acoustic scale to Hubble scale, and other quantities at multiple redshifts. Our findings indicate that the model performs better than a host of phantom dark energy models, as evidenced by the decay rate of the parameter $\delta$ and the behavior of the fluid with and without friction at early stages. When the bulk viscous friction is present, the model exhibits the following differences: the fluid's equation of state transitions from below to above a certain value of the parameter $\delta$, and we observe the reversed behavior of the fluid with and without friction at early stages in the space of the parameter $\delta$.

We present an easy-to-understand proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of Lorentz spaces, thereby confirming an earlier study by Bourgain and Li.

Recently, large text-conditioned generative diffusion models have received considerable attention for their impressive ability to generate detailed images from text input alone, yet they often produce low-fidelity artwork lacking the quality seen in traditional artistic styles. To capitalize on the benefits of diffusion models while achieving higher image quality, we introduce a novel approach that combines the stable diffusion model with external artistic influences. Our methodology involves guiding the diffusion process with image editing steers derived from various artistic styles, resulting in refined, high-resolution images that incorporate the desired styles. Additionally, we have developed multiple technical innovations that enable our approach to work effectively: introducing lossless latent space manifolds for artistic styles, developing a simple yet powerful method to transfer existing images onto this new manifold, and designing a real-world camera model to ensure that generated images display natural, high-fidelity textures. The success of our approach is demonstrated through a wide range of artistic style transfers and the generation of high-resolution, detailed images from raw latent space inputs.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, both of which can be learned through unsupervised methods. Experimental findings show that the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis results in improved steganographic performance with regard to capacity-distortion metrics.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective interactions, such as $|\kappa_{e,S}|^2<1.1\times10^{-10}$ and $|\lambda^{'}_{e,S}|^2<1.4\times10^{-9}$ at the 95% confidence level.

High-resolution observations of the solar photosphere reveal tiny magnetic bright points, associated with extremely strong magnetic fields, present throughout the solar cycle. These features, extensively detected in solar images, play a significant role in understanding the solar atmosphere's behavior in terms of energy transfer from the photosphere to the corona. This study aimed to examine the size, speed, and distribution patterns of magnetic bright points in the solar photosphere, using datasets from the SOT/Hinode and HiFI/GREGOR telescopes, to gain insights into their characteristics and movements. Employing an automated algorithm to detect magnetic bright points, we analyzed two datasets, resulting in a total of 437,827 detected features, each associated with a position, speed, and size measurement. By applying a non-parametric method, we discovered evidence of two distinct size distributions among magnetic bright points, presenting possible scenarios for their origin and implying the presence of two-component distributions among these solar phenomena. Furthermore, our analysis revealed consistent patterns in the size, speed, and acceleration of magnetic bright points across observed datasets.

Human vision can distinguish objects and actions using spatial or temporal data, but integrating these aspects remains unclear. This study demonstrates how the human visual system can effectively combine spatial and motion information, enabling recognition in scenarios where individual sources are insufficient. Researchers achieved this insight by analyzing'minimal videos' - brief clips that facilitate reliable object, part, and action recognition, but are unrecognizable when spatial or temporal constraints are compromised. Unlike existing deep networks, humans exhibit more adept performance in these complex configurations, highlighting missing dynamic vision mechanisms in current models.

Dark particles interacting through Abelian gauge symmetries and ordinary matter through kinetic mixing result in the manifestation of broken $U(1)$ magnetic monopoles in our observable universe as milli-magnetically charged entities confined under electromagnetism. However, the strength of their dark magnetic interactions with ordinary matter is significantly constrained by observations of galaxy halo ellipticities. Furthermore, the ground state of dark monopoles initially stable and chargeless becomes quantum mechanically unstable under an external magnetic field, potentially releasing energy on a galactic scale. If the dark monopoles' contribution to the local dark matter density is substantial, their galactic-scale decay can lead to energy extraction from the galactic magnetic field, effectively revising an existing constraint and imposing stricter limits on their magnetic interactions with ordinary matter.

The rapidly evolving Earth's atmosphere impacts various sectors, including transportation, agriculture, and energy, thus accurate weather forecasting is highly recommended. This paper addresses the table forecasting challenge in the Weather Research and Training (WrT) dataset, which contains historical weather data and predicts future weather patterns for aviation decision-making. Given the intricate relationships within spacetime weather data, we propose a cutting-edge Transformer network to incorporate relative positional information, focusing on local temporal and atmospheric contexts. The model's core lies in utilizing a shifted window cross-attention mechanism, which selectively aggregates information from relevant time segments and atmospheric layers, enhancing the prediction accuracy for time series and multi-dimensional weather data. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed SWC-Net outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, achieving a 33% increase in prediction accuracy, and showcases its robustness through ablation and visualization studies.

In models that expand on the electroweak sector, a basis can be found where the symmetry prevents coupling, leading to viable dark matter candidates. By investigating three-Higgs-doublet models with an $S_3$ symmetry, researchers discovered two candidates for dark matter, associated with each doublet. Notably, however, one candidate is always in a complex that's not stable under the symmetry, whereas the other can exist as a singlet or a real-determinant doublet. When the former candidate's decay is facilitated by a relevant operator within the framework, it's possible that its mass can be as low as a few GeV; otherwise, this mass is expected to be higher, potentially exceeding a few hundred GeV. Meanwhile, the second candidate's mass is expected to be greater than the $W$ boson's mass. Additionally, researchers found that while the first candidate's existing and novel decay modes demonstrate that its dark matter mass can be constrained by both the mono-photon search and the invisible decay of the $Z$ boson, the second candidate primarily interacts through weak gauge bosons in both its existing and newly-introduced decays, aligning it with mono-photon searches in the relevant mass range.

A comprehensive study on the PPT square conjecture is presented with a notable achievement: the PPT square conjecture's validity has been rigorously demonstrated for the case involving finite-dimensional space.

Intracellular transportation is crucial for delivering vital substances to complex branched neural structures, enabling their survival, adaptation to their environment, and normal functioning. Abnormal transportation has been linked to various neurode disorders, suggesting the need for optimal transportation models to aid diagnosis and treatment. However, developing such models is challenging due to the complex non-linear relationships between transportation parameters, the intricate structure of neural cells, and the requirement for rapid solutions. To address these issues, a new approach involves formulating an optimization problem constrained by partial differential equations to describe transportation phenomena in complex neural geometries. By applying the adjoint method, this problem can be efficiently solved, and multiple transportation parameters can be efficiently estimated through least squares minimization. The proposed method is versatile and can be applied to various cellular and neural axon geometries.

Billion-dollar losses inflicted by banking fraud across the globe make graph-based fraud detection in transactions increasingly significant. In analyzing transaction patterns, researchers utilize graphs to identify novel and complex schemes. This research aims to identify real-world transaction network patterns, specifically network motifs within a heterogenous transaction dataset. We also present a method for generating genuine banking transaction graphs via randomization. The outcome of our preliminary analysis indicates that extracting network motifs can reveal meaningful and understandable patterns within the data.

In a black hole-white dwarf binary system, we examine electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted during a process where a white dwarf loses mass to a black hole through tidal forces. We simulate this scenario using a quantum hydrodynamic model and represent the white dwarf as a zero-temperature Bose-Fermi droplet. When the white dwarf approaches its point of closest approach to the black hole, it loses a portion of its mass, causing the black hole to experience an influx of matter. This mass accretion leads to the generation of intense bursts of electromagnetic and gravitational radiation, with spectra that can be described using a power law. Notably, the radiation is optimized when the white dwarf and black hole are nearly equal in mass and the binary system has a minimal amount of orbital angular momentum. This optimal scenario occurs for black holes with masses ranging from approximately 1.35 to 3.0 solar masses when paired with white dwarfs having masses of 0.90 to 1.20 solar masses for certain chosen coupling constants.

Jim\'enez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) introduced the "symmetric Tversky ratio models" with parameters $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ where $\alpha$ ranges between 0 and 1 and $\beta$ is greater than 0. The inverse of each $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ function yields what we term the "asymmetric Tversky distance" $D_{\alpha,\beta}$, also expressed as the ratio of differences between sets' cardinalities divided by $\beta$ plus the alpha-weighted sum of the cardinalities of the two-minute clocks. For $\alpha$ equal to 0.5, the asymmetric Tversky distance reduces to the Jaccard distance; otherwise, it diverges from it. However, if we fix $\alpha$ and let $\beta$ approach 0, the asymmetric Tversky distance $D_{\alpha,0}$ turns into what we call the "augmented Ball distance" $D_{\alpha}$, which is related to the normalized Shannon entropy. Thus, we generalize the Jaccard distance to the $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ family and, conversely, specialize it to the $D_{\alpha}$ family, which itself is a generalized version of the Jaccard distance.

Modern motion deblurring methods based on deep learning utilize paired synthetic data for training frameworks, aiming to directly convert blurry inputs to clear outputs. However, the success of these methods heavily relies on high-quality synthetic blurry data available only before training, a constraint that becomes impractical with large datasets. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an on-the-fly data augmentation technique to create blurry inputs dynamically during training and testing. A novel approach using a conditional generator that predicts a time-dependent motion blur curve allows for the creation of these inputs. As a result, our method not only achieves superior deblurring performance on standard benchmarks and real-world videos but also demonstrates robustness against various challenges, including non-blur-shift movements, low-light conditions, and image degradations due to camera noise.

Hebbian theory aims to explain how brain cells modify their responses to stimuli, ultimately leading to the ability to learn. A notable aspect of Hebbian learning is its ability to occur independently, without requiring external feedback. This concept is further explored in a research paper, which outlines a novel, chemical-based system capable of exhibiting autonomous Hebbian learning through multiple input channels. This artificial neural network model is based on a simple chemical reaction network and is demonstrated to identify patterns in the input data it receives, even in the presence of noisy signals. In addition to the fundamental reaction network, the researchers propose more complex variations that integrate external components into the system to enhance its learning capabilities.

The ultrapower of any ordered set is created as a refined version of the set itself by taking into account infinite sequences of elements from it. This process involves dividing the sequences into classes according to a set of rules defined by an ultrafilter, leading to a set that always satisfies a fundamental property of ordered sets. It turns out that a set's openness determines its ability to fulfill the open completeness property in the refined version, whereas its original cardinality dictates whether the refined version is complete.

Scientific breakthroughs in data-driven science increasingly rely on applying sophisticated AI models to comprehensive, discipline-specific datasets. However, the computational resources required to evaluate every possible model against a large dataset are excessively expensive, rendering them impractical to execute. As a result, existing benchmarking approaches utilize select, representative datasets, but this limited method restricts extensive analysis and introduces bias towards models that perform well on those chosen datasets, thus overlooking each feature of the remaining data. In response to these challenges, we aim to establish a new framework that dynamically characterizes datasets in a manner sensitive to computational constraints, thereby enabling the identification of relevant sub-sets of the original data and simultaneously assessing the performance of models against the entire data set simultaneously.

Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture asserts that every graph with t colors includes a complete graph with t vertices. This has been reinforced by another theory suggesting if a given graph is assigned t colors, where a certain set of its vertices uses every possible color, then that graph must have a complete graph with t vertices within it. This more robust idea has been tested with success for the case of t = 4. This result holds further implications for 5-colored graphs; specifically, we can confirm a revised and more robust version of the original Hadwiger's conjecture for 5-colored graphs except in one specific instance - the K Killian graph.

This research introduces an advanced algorithm for efficiently recovering smooth graph signals through generalized correntropy, and a specific loss function is formulated accordingly. Derived from the aforementioned principle, the algorithm is developed further, and a variant leveraging kernel width adaptation is presented. Results indicate that this adaptive kernel width variant surpasses the fixed kernel approach. In addition, the research undertakes theoretical examinations of the algorithm's properties. Firstly, the analysis focuses on proving the cost function's convexity. Secondly, the stability of the algorithm is analyzed under uniform conditions. Lastly, the mean convergence of the algorithm is assessed. Furthermore, the computational complexity of the algorithm is analyzed. Experiments conducted using synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the superiority of the proposed algorithm over existing methods for adaptive graph signal recovery.

Theoretical investigations are conducted to design and control entangled atomic states formed through spin-changing collisions within a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate for use in a more robust atom interferometry capable of withstanding common technical problems like detector limitations. It is discovered through both analytical and numerical examinations of the spin-changing collision process that utilizing a small initial magnetization can produce a highly entangled state of Mach-Zehnder-type, which is resistant to detection errors and can be more effectively produced with lower magnetic field strengths than previously achievable. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that applying a controlled magnetic field pulse after the collision can refine the entanglement properties of the state, thereby enabling the production of both deeply entangled states resistant to detection errors and states with less entanglement that may be more useful in various atomic interferometry applications.

The purpose of this research paper is to derive optimal estimates for the first eigenvalue of the first Robin eigenvalue problem involving the anisotropic $p$-Laplace operator. This problem seeks to minimize a specific functional over all nonzero functions in the Sobolev space, and involves several variables and constants, including $p$, a bounded mean convex domain $\Omega$ in $N$-dimensional space, and a smooth norm $F$ on this space. We discovered new lower and upper bounds for this eigenvalue problem based on the first eigenvalue of a one-dimensional nonlinear problem. Specifically, for positive $\beta$ we proved a lower bound and for negative $\beta$ we proved an upper bound. Furthermore, for positive $\beta$ we were able to derive a lower bound for the first eigenvalue of the problem, and for negative $\beta$ we were able to derive an upper bound. In the case of positive $\beta$, the first eigenfunction of the problem converges weakly in the Sobolev space to a nonzero constant function in any minimization sequence for the first eigenvalue. This result implies a lower bound for the first eigenvalue of the problem. In the case of negative $\beta$, the first eigenfunction of the problem changes sign. Furthermore, for sufficiently small values of $\beta$ the first eigenfunction of the problem attains its sign outside the boundary of the domain and its first derivative vanishes at the boundary of the domain. This result implies

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to buried within vast network architectures. We propose an intuitive analysis based on the concept of matched filtering to illustrate how GCNNs operate at their core, matched filtering aligning with the network's name. This straightforward framework effectively captures key features, enabling translation between filter matching and graph convolution formulations. Consequently, our analysis sheds light on previously obscure GCNN components, such as learning optimal graph smoothing functions, and validates the empirical success of residual learning and non-linearity in graph input.

A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven costly and impractical to obtain. This paper proposes a novel self-training technique that mitigates this data annotation constraint by leveraging the parser's own output to improve performance. Specifically, the Deep Contextualized Self-training algorithm integrates external sequence models, derived from the parser's application to unlabelled data, into the parser using a sophisticated weighting system. Comprehensive experiments have been conducted across multiple languages, demonstrating that our technique successfully boosts the parser's accuracy even in scenarios where limited labelled data is available.

We've investigated the transition form factors $f_+(q^2)$ and $f_-(q^2)$ [alternatively $f_0(q^2)$] for exclusive semileptonic $B	o D\ell
u_\ell$ $(\ell=e,\mu,	au)$ decays using the standard light-front quark model based on light-front quantization. Conventionally, $f_+(q^2)$ can be determined without considering troublesome elements, but $f_-(q^2)$ typically includes such difficulties. However, our study reveals in the Drell-Yan frame ($q^+=0$) that the results obtained using $(J^+, J^-)$ for $f_-(q^2)$ are equivalent to those derived from $(J^+, { f J}_\perp)$ without including treacherous components. Furthermore, our calculations provided the form factors and branching ratios for $B	o D\ell
u_\ell$ $(\ell=e,\mu,	au)$ decays, enabling an evaluation of the first precision weak correction for $B	o D\ell
u_\ell$ $(\ell=e,\mu)$ beyond the Drell-Yan frame.

Theories of supersymmetric Yang-Mills with algebra so(4N) can have non-trivial, invertible-defying symmetries. By utilizing holographic duality, we can determine the branes equivalent to these symmetries, and deduce the fusion principles for the symmetries through brane dynamics.

Currently, Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) stands out as the most promising approach to tackle decision problems within PTIME (polynomial time) complexity, having demonstrated the capability to be contained within PTIME and yet unseparated from it. A prominent challenge in CPT research involves establishing its ability to solve problems defined by their circuits, which raises the question of distinguishing non-empty sets specified by oracles. In this study, we explore the boundaries of CPT applied to symmetric graph problems, specifically considering the Cai-Furer-Immerman (CFI) graphs class, which is known to be decisionable through quantified logic on graphs but also accessible through polynomial time algorithms. Our contributions involve designing a CPT formula to determine if a given graph exhibits more than half its maximum clique size within the input property, a characteristic shared by CFI graphs as well as those solvable via polynomial time algorithms. This achievement addresses the aforementioned query and extends the CPT containment within the class of all superfeasible graphs, a known PTIME- CPT distinction. Additionally, our work also yields a distinct CPT formula for identifying if a binary matrix contains a non-empty matrix with a specific determinant value. This distinctness holds within the context of the monotone cone of random oracle results.

In a compound exhibiting quantum phenomena similar to those in a proposed phase in 3D topological insulators, the transformation from an insulating state to a metallic state was investigated through x+o variations of a key element in the pyrochlore iridates series (Eu1-xBix)2Ir2O7 using HXPES. This technique enabled the distinction to be made and time resolved analysis to be carried out on the driving force behind the phase transition, demonstrating that the phase transition is caused by the reduction of insulating properties and the generation of a p-d hybridization energy similar to that of a 120-degree ordered antiferromagnetic state in reference compounds that do not contain Bi. This finding is supported by the analysis of an insulating state to a metallic state in (Eu0.5Bi0.5)2Ir2O7 through the use of HXPES, where the Bi 4f levels in the material exhibit an abrupt shift during the phase transition. Additionally, Bi was found to be soluble within a specific concentration range in this study.

Consider a metric space ${\mathfrak M}=({\mathcal M},\rho)$ and a Banach space $X$, with a set-valued mapping $F$ that maps ${\mathcal M}$ to the family ${\mathcal K}_m(X)$ of compact convex subsets of $X$ of dimension $m$ or less. Our recent joint research with Charles Fefferman established a principle that enables the existence of a Lipschitz selection for $F$, which is a mapping $f:{\mathcal M}\to X$ that satisfies $f(x)\in F(x)$ for every $x\in{\mathcal M}$. This paper presents alternative proofs for the existence criterion in the case of a 2-dimensional mapping $F$. Additionally, it proposes algorithms to find a Lipschitz selection for such a mapping, which are illustratively applied to several concrete problems.

Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for $i$ ranging from 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We present a general lower limit for the likelihood that a given random variable $U$ will be less than another, denoted as $U_Q$, where $U_Q$ has a uniform distribution within the range [0,1]. This established criterion enables the generation of specific 'cyclic' and 'nontransitive' n-tuples, which in turn allows us to answer previously unaddressed questions regarding necessary conditions for 'cyclic' and 'nontransitive' n-tuples, including those with integer values greater than 3.

Many software systems have adjustable settings through run-time parameters, such as input options, which often lead to an infinite number of possible configurations. Focusing on such systems, this research investigates whether these numerous potential settings can be reduced to a more manageable number through analysis of the system's source code. It also examines whether these specialized settings can effectively address users' needs, improving the system's usability. A comparative study between a specialized system, made collaborative filtering-enabled by source code analysis, and an unspecialized system, configured through user input, revealed substantial differences in performance and efficiency. However, finding that the specialized system's optimized settings sometimes deviated from the most effective options, the researchers proposed a novel algorithm, ConfigOpt, to identify the most suitable parameters within a reduced search space, thus striking a balance between specialization and solution effectiveness. A statistical analysis of a large dataset confirmed that ConfigOpt consistently found top-ranking settings compared to the original source-code-specialized and user-configured approaches, thus highlighting the benefits of specializing configuration spaces through source-code analysis.

Light dark matter particles, particularly those weighing less than a GeV, offer an attractive option over heavier, weakly-interacting massive particles. Directly detecting such lightweight particles, however, poses a significant challenge. But if the recoil of a struck nucleus leads to electron ionization, even if the recoil itself is too subtle to be measured, it could still be possible to detect the released electron. This process has been found to significantly boost the sensitivity of direct detection experiments to sub-GeV dark matter. In the present, experiments set global records, and future experiments are likely to reach the cross-sections critical to understanding thermal equilibrium.

This paper proposes a method to produce the most connected pairs of qubit states
via an anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction system, resulting in maximally entangled
anti-polariton qubits. The study finds that in the initial absence of any photons,
the quantum fluctuations of the anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction behave in the opposite
direction of the standard Jaynes-Cummings interaction process and the rate at which
these states become entangled has a similar pattern in both processes. Furthermore,
utilizing this maximally connected state and entanglement swapping, a near perfect
transfer of an atomic quantum state via quantum teleportation is demonstrated.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health monitoring and wearable devices have identified signal denoising and IBI estimation as a significant area of focus. Recent breakthroughs have involved the use of deep learning, which has significantly improved signal quality and diagnostic accuracy, far exceeding previous limitations. A novel deep learning approach is being presented that uses a Tiramisu autoencoder to effectively remove motion artifact and make ECG signals more interpretable even during high-impact motion. By achieving accurate denoising and IBI estimation, this approach accelerates diagnostic processes and achieves better results. Notably, our technique has successfully estimated IBIs from ECG signals with an error rate of 9.67%, including significant artifact induced by high-impact motion.

We analyze large deviations of power input by an active force on an Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle (AOUP) within or outside a confinement. Analytical calculations of the rate function are done for the free particle in any dimension using a saddle-point expansion. Additionally, a direct numerical approach via solution of the AOUP equations is performed, alongside a method using Legendre-Fenchel transform of the scaled cumulant generating function obtained via extensive simulations. Results for the free particle exhibit asymptotically linear behavior on both sides of the bifurcation parameter value marking the transition from active to passive behavior. In confinement, a phase diagram in parameter space was created through extensive simulations, exhibiting three regimes. Calculations of large deviations for any location in this parameter space are performed via direct evaluation of the AOUP equations and compared with the obtained rate functions to uncover relationships between work and energy in these regimes.

This research introduces HUMBI, a large dataset featuring diverse human body
expressions captured from multiple perspectives. The database includes complex
sequences of body poses involving intricate interactions of two to five limbs.
HUMBI was recorded using high-resolution cameras that captured both 2D and 3D body
renderings. The dataset's comprehensive labeling enables the examination of rich
body languages within the context of body pose, orientation, and movement. Our
analysis reveals the limitations of current single-view datasets in capturing
body expression complexity and the benefits of using multiview approaches. To drive
progress in this area, we're launching the HUMBI Challenge, which focuses on
using 3D body models to create engaging, short video clips conveying clear
emotional messages. The challenge's benchmark and baseline models are detailed in a
separate paper. The HUMBI dataset is accessible at https://humbi-data.github.io/.

Despite the growing need for models in non-English languages, natural language processing has long been Anglo-centric, and translating neural models between languages can be costly and time-consuming in terms of data labeling, development time, and expertise. We propose a universal approach to effortlessly and effectively transfer neural models from English to other languages. Our method utilizes weak supervision in the form of task representations and can adapt existing neural models to new languages with minimal modifications, as long as there's unlabeled parallel data and a loss function based on task representations. We put our framework to the test by transferring an English sentiment classifier to three foreign languages and discovered that it surpasses the performance of numerous strong baselines while matching or even exceeding the results obtained through more resource-intensive and expensive methods. Moreover, our framework successfully captures rich, semantically significant representations across languages despite the absence of direct supervision.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, utilizing a compact model that efficiently achieves high-quality super-resolution with minimal computational requirements. This paper enhances BasicVSR in two key areas: propagation and alignment, allowing for increased flexibility in the original design without significantly increasing computational complexity. A proposed new alignment module also enables greater control over feature interaction across frame hierarchies. As a result, the improved BasicVSR model delivers superior visual quality and more adaptable advancements to similar architectures.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task and allowing them to be shared across tasks, while
still using a unified policy network, yields better outcomes and reduces
interference.

We have improved the performance of heat engines working within specific timeframes, employing a time-varying energy function in conjunction with experimentally grounded limitations on the bath temperature and the scale factor. A broadly applicable geometric proof has demonstrated that the maximum efficiency in these systems can be achieved by alternating between the maximum and minimum permissible temperatures and scale factor values. For situations where the scale factor range is restricted and the system's thermal state closely matches its equilibrium values at temperature plateaus, this protocol also ensures maximum output energy production. These findings are valid for a wide range of physical systems, including an overdamped heat engine driven by a particle in an optical tweezers setup characterized by a scale factor related to the stiffness.

This research proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing the impact of combined hurricane and storm surge events on large power grids. To simulate real-world hurricane scenarios, the study generates probabilistic storm paths based on historical data, and corresponding storm surge situations are developed based on actual hurricane parameters. To assess potential losses, the study employs a quantitative metric that estimates total load reduction, and these outcomes are calculated using a simulated model of the 2000-bus Texas power system superimposed onto a real-world map of sea-level rise vulnerabilities.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

We define new families of parametrized piecewise affine transformations on 2D and 3D spaces as generalized versions of the heterochaos baker map, initially developed as simplified models for unstable dimension variability in complex systems. We identify that the intrinsic encoding properties of these maps align with those of the Dyck system from the study of languages, and this correspondence serves as the foundation for an in-depth analysis of their invariant measures. Through initial investigation, we confirm the existence of two distinct ergodic measures with maximal entropy for these generalized baker maps, and also reveal the underlying cause for the failure of certain entropy-based approaches.

Following the groundbreaking detection of the Higgs boson in 2012, the field of particle physics has entered an exciting period. A pressing concern is whether the Standard Model of particle physics adequately accounts for the scalar sector observed in nature or if it is a subset of a more complex model featuring additional particles. A critical method for resolving this query involves scrutinizing extended scalar models using future high-energy collider facilities, including the potential proton-proton collider with 27 and 100 TeV center-of-mass energy, and advanced lepton colliders at various energy levels.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network's autoregressive structure is modified by splitting it into quasi-periodic and residual components. Secondly, the QPNet pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural network is designed with more parameters for the frequency range determined by the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) size and is applied to both the input and previous autoregressive predictions. Experimental evaluations using the LJSpeech dataset demonstrate that QPNet surpasses WN in terms of mean opinion score (MOS) and is more versatile in terms of speaker and language variability.

Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF), the dominant method, have become an integral part of our daily lives as consumers. However, their limitations become apparent when dealing with recommendation data due to the complexities and idiosyncrasies of user preferences. Researchers attempted to overcome these challenges by integrating CF with Biclustering techniques. This research aims to evaluate the efficacy of Biclustering approaches for CF, analyzing various algorithmic decisions, and identifies key principles for high-performing Biclustering-based CF methods. As a result, this work proposes USBFC, a CF method leveraging Biclustering that develops user-tailored models from statistically meaningful and strongly consistent rating patterns across subspaces of shared user preferences. When evaluated on real-world datasets, USBCF outperforms existing CF methods in predictive accuracy and surpasses previously proposed CF methods with improved coverage and subspace cohesion.

Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators that better reflect a star's magnetic behavior is essential for distinguishing these signals from a planet's Doppler signal. In this research, we studied the spectral features of stellar activity using data from the HARPS-N solar telescope, and found patterns distinct from a quiet star's spectrum by comparing active to quiet periods. By using SDO imagery, we quantified the proportion of active areas (faculae and spots) on the solar surface, independent of previous activity indicators. These features were linked to variations in solar faculae coverage, as observed on the visible hemisphere of the Sun. Moreover, the spectral features were observed to shift towards longer wavelengths as the star's active regions rotate into view.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance's temperature dependence, distinguishing Majorana from other types of zero-energy peaks. Our theoretical work on the BCS model shows that Majorana peaks survive high resistance changes, whereas other types of zero-energy peaks fade. The non-zero temperature tunneling conductance of Majorana peaks remains unaffected, differing from the situation at zero temperature where it vanishes with increased resistance. Our approach addresses the issue of accurately identifying Majorana charge zero-energy peaks in the presence of high resistance contacts and non-zero temperature.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence.

Existing approaches to image editing tasks like color grading often yield multiple
possible outcomes rather than a single definitive result, as numerous different
styles can produce similar results. Current machine learning-based methods tend to
focus on optimizing a single style or set of control parameters for a given input,
which typically selected arbitrarily or required the user to choose. This style
selection was typically facilitated by providing users with a pair of images, as
the difference in style between the pair can be learned and applied to new inputs.
However, many practical applications involve users having a single image and desiring
a different tone or style. We propose learning a distinct "forward" network to
automatically determine the style from such a pair, which can then be used for
automated image editing. Since the reverse "inverse" network would require the
receipt of a varied set of training images for each specific style, we instead
develop a single universal inverse network that can handle any style through the
use of a specialized loss function incorporating the style of the pair. Our
universal inverse network can effectively reverse the effects of the forward
network, as demonstrated by the results achieved with the color grading task.

This technical report showcases the winning model of the AQTC task, recently introduced in the LOVEU challenge at CVPR 2022, where experts faced significant challenges in processing multi-step responses, multiple modalities, and dynamic button representations within video content. To overcome this, we developed a novel context-grounding module that enhances feature mapping using attention mechanisms. We further explored the effects of varying button counts, conducted ablation studies on different network architectures and video feature types, and attained a 2nd place ranking overall in the LOVEU track 3 competition. Notably, we achieved a 1st place ranking in two of the four evaluation metrics. Our open-source code is accessible via the repository link at https://github.com/jaykim9870/CVPR-22_LOVEU_unipyler.

This field research focuses on snow deposition dynamics by monitoring the atmosphere's flow patterns and snowflake trajectories in real time. A state-of-the-art, high-resolution imaging system is utilized to capture snowflakes in motion, mapping the flow patterns and detecting vortex formations above the ground. Concurrently, a high-resolution camera is employed to track individual snowflakes in a smaller sample area within the main field of view, revealing the connection between atmospheric turbulence and snowflake settling patterns. Our research reveals that as snowflakes interact with turbulence at critical velocities, their falling speed is greatly increased, a phenomenon not seen in prior studies. Images captured within the flow patterns show that snowflakes tend to concentrate near the base of vortex formations, moving preferentially downwards. High-resolution footage of these vortex formations provides quantitative evidence of accelerated snowflake speeds. This research provides robust evidence that a phenomenon called preferential sweeping is the primary cause of enhanced snow deposition in the atmosphere's lower layers.

A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. This framework is maintained through a process of mental updates, driven by discoveries. The theory has been successful in simulating real-world interactions within virtual environments but faces a significant obstacle: its application to real-world scenarios is hindered by the complexity of equating mental and sensory observations. This complication arises due to the need for continuous sensory data collection from the real world, making it challenging to match observations from the perceived reality to the detailed mental framework. The challenge can be overcome by employing a more detailed representation of the world, allocating a section for anticipated observations. This approach allows for the development of a deep active inference network that can be used for autonomous robot navigation. The network's effectiveness has been tested in a simulated delivery navigation scenario and is found to successfully apply the active inference theory to real-world scenarios, accurately estimating uncertainties and navigating successfully.

In experimental facilities specializing in high energy physics, nuclear physics, and cosmology, the task of processing large amounts of data in real-time is proving to be a substantial hurdle. As an alternative to standard compression methods, the use of machine learning algorithms has gained attention for real-time data compression. Yet, data sets generated from scientific endeavors often comprise vast 3D data sets characterized by sparse activity. Consequently, direct applications of popular compression methods along with standard convolutional neural networks demonstrate incompetence. This paper introduces the Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE), an innovative model designed specifically for the efficient compression of 3D sparse data. By employing a dual-head structure, BCAE encodes data into a more compact format while simultaneously generating sparse feature maps for each dimension, ultimately resulting in improved compression ratios and error rates.

Utilizing Finzi's gravity theory that enhances interactions at large scales, we analyze galaxy clusters from a thermodynamic perspective, establishing a statistical model to derive thermodynamic equations and comparing clustering behavior with Newtonian gravity. We also explore the general distribution function's behavior as the clustering parameter varies in strength, with the finding that phase transitions are feasible but only occur at extremely low temperatures.

A type of convex geometric hypergraph, known as cgh, comprises a set of subsets originating from strictly convex point sets in the plane. In this study, researchers explore a specific type of problem associated with cghs: saturation problems that correspond to earlier studied extremal issues. Using a mathematical approach, the study determines the maximum capacity of certain geometrically separated groups of points and establishes an exact value for a specific instance, as well as approximate values for seven out of eight possible geometric hypergraph configurations up to a specific level of accuracy, and a related but less accurate figure for the eighth configuration.

To gain a better understanding of the relative contributions of different processes, the angular distributions and energy spectra of $\alpha$ and deuterons resulting from breakup, transfer, and incomplete fusion have been measured and calculated. Cross-sections for the $^6$Li + $^{51}$V system were experimentally measured at energies near the Coulomb barrier, with theoretical estimates obtained through calculations with the finite range coupled reaction method using the \textsc{FRESCO} code. Calculations indicated that the cross-sections from various reaction channels including non-capture breakup and 1 proton, 1 neutron, and 1 deuteron transfer, compound nuclear decay by $\gamma$-ray, and incomplete fusion to $^3$He together account for the observed angular distributions and cross-sections of $\alpha$ and deuterons.

A previously overlooked ability in bio-inspired snake robots is dynamic vertical climbing. A novel locomotion technique mimicking the Pacific Lamprey's movement has been discovered, which enables a robot to navigate on flat surfaces while climbing at near-vertical inclines. A simplified model has been created to analyze the correlation between robot motion and actuation, resulting in the development of a new, adaptable robot inspired by the Pacific Lamprey. The new robot, called Trident, successfully demonstrates dynamic vertical climbing at speeds of up to 4.8 cm/s and can also move horizontally at 9 cm/s. Furthermore, its climbing strides can be extended to a height of over 3 times its body length, a feat of "double-feeding" that could be beneficial in difficult-to-navigate environments.

This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework designed to identify the most effective combinations of treatments in cases of colon cancer-induced immune response. An Itō stochastic process models the colon cancer dynamics, whose probabilistic evolution is governed by the Fokker-Planck equation. To identify optimal treatment combinations, an open-loop control optimization issue is proposed. Simulation results demonstrating the use of Doxorubicin chemotherapy and IL-2 immunotherapy validate the introduced framework.

Optimizing wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication success depends heavily on minimizing excessive interference through effective device scheduling. Traditional scheduling methods mainly prioritize maximizing throughput and fairness without considering the timeliness of received data. This paper presents a novel D2D link scheduling strategy that balances both Age of Information (AoI) and throughput by employing a packet replacement policy, which ensures fair link activation. Analytically derived expressions demonstrate how the network's overall AoI and throughput are affected under complex spatio-temporal interference. Furthermore, a neural network is designed to learn an optimal mapping between the network's state and the desired AoI/throughput ratio. Through extensive simulations, the proposed neural network is shown to successfully generalize new scenarios not included in its training, outperforming traditional scheduling methods.

Moffatt first discussed the concept of helicity in a fluid without viscosity in reference [25] and explored its preservation in the case of barotropic, compressible flow with smooth solutions. This paper demonstrates that weak solutions to this system in a specific mathematical space ensure the conservation of helicity. Additionally, similar results were found for both homogeneous incompressible Euler equations and the surface quasi-geostrophic equation.

The researchers in a particular study extended the solutions found in complex geometric optics to a related system of equations, which was initially investigated in contexts of electrical impedance tomography and the integrable Davey-Stewartson II equations. They determined that certain patterns of geometric optics in the given system correspond to distinct solutions of the equations under certain conditions. By analyzing the patterns and the concepts of light reflection and transmission, the authors evaluated the solutions' asymptotic behavior as one of two possible scenarios, based on whether the angle of incidence is greater or less than a particular critical value. Subsequently, the reflection coefficient was calculated based on this analysis. Moreover, the authors proposed that as the third-order parameter in the equations approaches zero, the solutions and their asymptotic behavior approach those found in a related system of equations, which was initially investigated in contexts of electrical impedance tomography and the integrable Davey-Stewartson II equations.

Calculations involving the orbital dynamics of merging compact binary systems
reveal that the binary's initial orbital position and alignment strongly influence
the gravitational waves produced.  Most of these analyses presume circular orbits
and a fixed alignment, but a novel approach allows for the investigation of
binary systems that maintain small eccentricities and varied alignments at the time
of detection.  A mathematical framework has been established to determine the
range of initial conditions that lead to a specified level of eccentricity at the
time of detection, and a corresponding algorithm has been developed to accurately
calculate the range of initial conditions for a given binary system at each stage
of evolution down to the point where gravitational waves are detectable.  A
combination of this framework and the algorithm enables the estimation of the
distributions of initial orbital positions and alignments for a given binary system
as it approaches the point where gravitational waves are detectable, and it is
expected that this method will be useful in further studies of the binary's
evolution.

A proposed innovation combines the benefits of X-ray free-electron laser oscillators (XFELOs) and the undulator taper technique to create a groundbreaking X-ray laser. This is made possible by using an XFELO to seed a free-electron laser (FEL) amplifier with a specially tailored electron beam. The unique characteristics of the beam allow for the tail to be within the gain bandwidth of XFELO, generating a lasing seed that's used for further amplification, while the leading part of the beam, outside XFELO's gain bandwidth, can still be utilized in the FEL amplifier. The suitability of naturally occurring "double-horn" beam current and residual energy chirp from a chicane compressor has also been identified. The outcome is potentially record-breaking levels of nearly terawatt X-ray pulses with superior shot-to-shot stability, paving the way for groundbreaking research across various fields.

Event identification is crucial for informed decision-making in graph data analysis systems.  Graph-based machine learning has made notable advancements lately, but detecting events in evolving networks still poses difficulties for current frameworks. Real-life occurrences typically involve sudden changes in network behavior patterns. Current methods for dynamic node representations are ineffective at capturing event-driven network changes.  To address these limitations, we propose a new approach, called DyGED, for recognizing events in evolving networks using a combination of temporal self-attention and structural awareness.  Through extensive testing with diverse datasets, we demonstrate that DyGED consistently outperforms alternative methods in accuracy, achieving up to an 8.5% improvement.  Notably, it also offers improved scalability compared to the best-performing models, along with insightful case studies that highlight its key features.

The solutions of the Guderley problem involving an imploding shock wave in an ideal gas are examined, focusing on how a power law initial density distribution affects the accelerating shock. This is achieved through in-depth analysis of self-similar solutions and their similarity exponents under different symmetry conditions and varying parameters of adiabatic index and spatial density exponent. Moreover, we show that these solutions can be accurately reproduced using a shock-fitting method, thereby validating this approach in a wide range of scenarios.

The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by reducing the opacity of these systems through the provision of explanations. In this paper, we will explore the interconnection between explainable AI and requirements engineering. The challenges in the XAI field will be highlighted and solutions proposed, with a framework and future research directions on how requirements engineering can aid in addressing these difficulties.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histopathological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved diagnostic accuracy in this field. However, training such models necessitates vast collections of annotated histopathological data, which is currently in short supply. To help bridge this gap, we've developed UniToPatho, a comprehensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images. This dataset supports the classification of colorectal polyps into benign, neoplastic, and invasive subcategories, as well as the grading of adenomas based on increasing levels of dysplasia. Comparing our results with the current state-of-the-art dataset from the "WoS: The Challenge" classification competition revealed substantial improvements across all tasks. This research was conducted in collaboration with Azienda Universitaria Spedali Civili and supported by grant contract 873850.

In the context of zero-error source coding, our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source symbols can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source sequence is measured relative to its prior knowledge, with this measurement maximized over various source distributions. When the adversary follows a specific model where they only make a single guess and can perfectly match their guess to the true sequence, this measurement is known as the maximal leakage in literature and can be expressed as the maximum min-entropy leakage. We establish a comprehensive single-letter representation of the optimal normalized leakage in this adversarial scenario, along with a stochastic coding method that reaches this optimum. Interestingly, our analysis shows that both the optimal leakage and optimal compression rates are attainable by certain deterministic coding strategies, where these goals can be concurrently achieved. We refer to such codes as leakages-free zero-error source codes. Furthermore, we extend our investigation to adversaries that make multiple guesses, offering upper and lower bounds on the optimal leakage in this scenario. Our study brings existing research on single-letter optimality in zero-error source coding, focusing on random codes, full-letter optimality in single-letter adversarial scenarios, focusing on deterministic codes, full-letter optimality in multiple-guess adversaries, focusing on random codes, full-letter optimality in multiple-guess adversaries, focusing on deterministic codes, full-letter optimality in independent memoryless sources, focusing on deterministic

Deep learning-trained generative models can be utilized as a prior in underdetermined inverse problems such as generating images from limited measurements, like partially acquired data. Nevertheless, prior models are often incompatible with the underlying measurement process. For example, training a generative model on real high-resolution images cannot utilize real low-resolution data as input. To address this issue, we propose MrSARP, a hierarchical generative prior that incorporates multiple levels of resolution to accommodate low-resolution input. The system comprises three main components: a base-level neural network that generates real high-resolution images, a mid-level component that produces intermediate-resolution features, and a post-processing step that refines the output. The system is applied to the super-resolution of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images and combines a conventional inverse problem solver with the learned prior. Experimental results demonstrate that MrSARP achieves better super-resolution performance compared to existing methods.

A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant employs a combined quantum-classical strategy to achieve approximate solutions for complex optimization issues.  To optimize a quantum circuit's parameters, we utilize a Bayesian approach as an auxiliary routine, evaluating its efficiency in contrast with alternative global optimizers.  The proposed technique leads to considerable reductions in circuit access frequency, essentially mitigating the expense of non-deterministic quantum processing.  The results show that the Bayesian approach consistently achieves high quality solutions, even with lower circuit evaluations, and it also generates more stable and predictable solutions compared to global optimizers.

A versatile method has been devised for determining the overlap area between two ellipses. The proposed approach relies on computing segment areas between the two ellipses, using a secant line that intersects each ellipse at given points. The Gauss-Green formula enables calculation of an ellipse sector area, with a triangle either added to or subtracted from this sector area to obtain the segment area. For calculating the overlap area of two ellipses, the areas of relevant sectors and polygons are combined. The algorithm identifies the intersection points of two general ellipses by utilizing Ferrari's quartic formula to solve a resulting polynomial formed by combining the two ellipse equations, allowing for handling all cases of intersection points, including none, one, two, three, or four points. The proposed method has been implemented in C and validated through numerous tests with diverse input ellipses, demonstrating its efficiency for applications involving multiple overlap area calculations in simulations.

Building upon the work by Wang et al. (2020) for reinforcement learning, we examine the continuous-time counterpart of Q-learning under the entropy-regularized exploratory process framework. This regularized process adds a simple method to address the role of exploration in reinforcement learning. We derive equations for the first two moments of the temporal difference (TD) error in continuous time. These equations are then used to develop a continuous-time Q-learning algorithm. We prove that this algorithm converges to the optimal policy when working under the exploratory process. Additionally, when the exploratory process vanishes, the algorithm converges to the optimal policy under the given reward structure. We validate our continuous-time Q-learning algorithm through simulations and compare it with the existing discrete-time Q-learning algorithm.

Quantum magnets' dynamical structure factor is a critical measurement, but making predictions for multi-dimensional models like Hubbard is complicated due to computational and theoretical constraints. We investigated magnetic excitations in the Hubbard model on a triangular lattice with longer-range hopping. Beginning with the 120-degree and striped patterns of magnetism, we used the self-consistent random phase approximation to determine magnon frequencies. We discovered that the Hubbard model with longer-range hopping exhibited a more extensive parameter range for magnetism than the corresponding 3D Heisenberg model with 12:1 hopping ratios. Our results showed a correlation between the spin density and the dynamical structure factor, allowing us to determine the spin density in the Hubbard model with longer-range hopping through a disordering approach. We found substantial agreement between our results for the dynamical structure factor and recent findings from Monte Carlo simulations.

Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise method that leverages in-depth anatomical knowledge of the spine to aid in accurate vertebrae localization and identification. By employing a novel key point localization model, this method enables efficient and accurate localization of vertebrae levels, which in turn serves as a foundation for an identification optimization model that incorporates anatomical constraints. Ultimately, this combined approach achieved superior results in the 2019 AI Challenge, garnering the top ranking in the validation set with a Dice score of 0.9856, and demonstrating its remarkable resilience against various adverse conditions.

Stochastic thermodynamics leverages Markovian jump processes to simulate spontaneous changes between quantifiable microscopic states. The flow rates of physical processes are calculated from the anti-symmetric transition measures defined on the network of states. The statistical behavior of these flow rates can be represented as normalized sums of path-wise products of transition matrices and temporal displacement operators. Although the average and variance of these averages are insensitive to the chosen starting point, their asymptotic distributions are influenced by the specific definition of this average. Consequently, varying the definition results in different forms of the central limit theorem application, leading to different assumptions for the likelihood of observing certain currents in nonequilibrium states. To rectify this issue, a correction must be applied to the estimated variance of the asymptotic distribution to achieve universal asymptotic normality, even in the presence of nonstationary Markovian processes.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

Two piezoelectric materials placed near each other can transfer energy across an intervening vacuum gap by sound waves. Our research provides a mathematical explanation for how this energy transfer occurs, and reveals that specific conditions allow for complete energy transfer between the materials. Furthermore, energy is transferred more efficiently when the two piezoelectric materials are identical, and occurs at precise resonant frequencies. When the materials have different properties, the energy transfer occurs over a wider frequency range and is less efficient, albeit still facilitated by the resonant properties of the coupled system.

We explore a cutting-edge method for optically manipulating polariton condensates at a microscale, relying on highly coherent fluids of semiconductor-based light-emitting systems. Theoretical research indicates that modern spatial light manipulation technologies can be employed to redirect and concentrate these polariton condensates away from their initial sources of excitation. By strategically modulating non-resonant energy beams, an underlying exciton reservoir is generated which red-shifts and intensifies the polariton emission, allowing the formation of micro-scale lens-shaped structures that can steer polariton wave propagation. Multiple approaches are suggested for controlling polariton flow and demonstrate the feasibility of producing robust and localized light-emitting systems isolated from negative reservoir-induced effects.

The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22b displays erratic patterns in transit best attributed to a dissipating debris cloud, with the formation process of this debris still unknown. Analyzing grain size and sublimation rate is essential in comprehending the environment that contributes to planetary disintegration. In this study, dual photometric data obtained through the Large Binocular Telescope, with wavelengths of 0.48 and 2.1 microns, are presented during a period of reduced dust activity, revealing a refined upper limit of the planet's radius of approximately 4500 km. Medium-depth transit observations also suggest particle sizes ranging from 0.5 to 1 micron, suggesting extremely high mass loss rates of about 3e8 kg/s, coherent with hydrodynamic escape theories. In contrast, explosive volcanic eruptions or other mechanisms generating this activity would demand exceptional geological activity levels. Combining these results with the maximum possible planetary size, our findings estimate the remaining lifespan of the exoplanet at approximately 370 million years; conversely, incorporating predictions from hydrodynamical models yields a remarkably reduced lifespan of only 21 million years.

We develop a novel algebro-geometric approach to studying the Milnor fibration and establish a significant condition for holomorphic function deformations to maintain the Milnor fibration intact. In consequence, we derive a strategy to divide the space of polynomials with a specified degree into discrete, localized segments where the diffeomorphism of the Milnor fibration remains unchanged within each category.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library focused on data analytics and linear algebra. Designed for.NET environments, this tool facilitates data preparation, feature engineering, and other data transformation operations. Developed atop.NET Standard 2.1 and compatible with.NET Core 3.0+, Daany consists of multiple VS projects that can be easily installed as a NuGet package. At its core, Daany utilizes the DataFrame data structure, complemented by data science and linear algebra capabilities, including time series decomposition (SSA, STL, ARIMA) and optimization methods (SGD). The library also integrates matrix and vector operations, as well as data plotting functionality. Daany's implementation bears similarities to Python's Pandas library.
